paras: The lynching of Henry Holloway took place on Tuesday, October 3, 1882, when a crowd seized Holloway, a young Black man accused of raping a white woman, at the end of a magistrates' hearing at Elkton in Giles County, Tennessee, and hanged him from the iron bridge over the Elk River. A short wire dispatch carried the story across the country within a day, and Tennessee papers openly approved the killing.

According to the Pulaski Citizen, Holloway was accused of going on Saturday night, September 30, to the house of a Mr. Rogers on Mrs. L. D. Suttle's place, nine miles south of Pulaski, and assaulting Mrs. Rogers, a woman of about fifty, while her husband was away. The next morning a posse headed by George Suttle, jr., found him in a thicket near his house playing cards with two other Black men and took him to Elkton. The preliminary hearing was put off until Tuesday, and the Milan Exchange reported that he was locked up from Sunday until then.

An attempt to lynch Holloway was made on Monday night, and his guards hid with him all night in a field. On Tuesday Mrs. Rogers identified him before the magistrates, Esqs. Hanserd and Hollon, who "pronounced him guilty"; a Maryland summary instead said the magistrate decided to commit him for trial. As soon as the judgment was announced the crowd rushed him, and Holloway grabbed Hanserd and dragged him down before he was pulled away.

The crowd took him to the high iron bridge over the Elk River, which the Milan Exchange put half a mile from the hearing, tied a rope from his neck to the railing and threw him over at about one o'clock. The Pulaski Citizen estimated that some two hundred people were present and said he clung to the railing but never spoke. His body hung for an hour before the magistrates had it cut down.

The Pulaski Citizen reported "comparatively very little excitement" over the hanging and said some Elkton citizens had been ready to defend Holloway had the hearing left any doubt of his guilt. No report of an inquest, arrest or indictment of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage.

The wire version, datelined Prospect, Tennessee, on October 4, ran in the Alexandria Gazette, the Washington Evening Star, the Memphis Public Ledger and, the next day, papers in Omaha, Dallas and Sacramento. Headlines ranged from the plain "Lynched" and "Hung From a Bridge" to "Short Shrift", "A Colored Brute Lynched" and "A Sable Fiend Lynched". The Washington Evening Critic ran it as "Gone to Embrace Guiteau", saying he had been taken from jail by an armed mob and had sung of Charley Guiteau before he died.

Tennessee papers endorsed the killing: the Pulaski Citizen, under "A Raper Lynched", called it "quick and sure and dreadful and just" and praised the crowd as "good men" doing a "righteous duty". The Milan Exchange called it "a deliberate and cool punishment", and the Winchester Home Journal ended its notice "So mote it be." By the following week syndicated roundups in Michigan and Dakota reduced it to a single line, a lynching at Elkton "for an outrage upon a white woman".

The wire dateline and several summaries placed the hearing at Prospect, while the county-seat Pulaski Citizen, the most detailed source, placed the hearing and hanging at Elkton. The Evening Critic's report of a song about Guiteau conflicts with the Pulaski Citizen, which said Holloway spoke only to ask for water and said nothing at the bridge.

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Holloway
bases: A crowd seized Henry Holloway, a Black man held on a rape accusation, as a magistrates' hearing ended and hanged him from a bridge (A5, A6, A9).

Holloway was hanged by a crowd (some two hundred present by the local account) that took him from magistrates and guards without lawful authority, as punishment for an alleged rape the papers called 'just' and 'righteous' (A6, A9, A20).
The Prospect wire dispatch (A5, A6) and the independent local account of the Pulaski Citizen (A9) agree that Holloway was seized after a hearing and hanged from a bridge on Tuesday, October 3, 1882.

accounts.gist: Holloway had a hearing before a magistrate, was pronounced guilty, and was then seized by a crowd and hanged from a bridge near by; the Evening Critic version says an armed mob took him from jail at Elkton and that he sang of Guiteau.

accounts.label: Pulaski Citizen (county-seat paper)
accounts.gist: A posse caught Holloway Sunday, guards hid him from a lynching party Monday night, and after magistrates Hanserd and Hollon pronounced him guilty Tuesday about two hundred men took him to the Elk River iron bridge and hanged him; he said nothing but asked for water.

accounts.label: Milan Exchange
accounts.gist: Places the alleged assault at Prospect, says he was locked up from Sunday to Tuesday, and that a crowd carried him to a bridge half a mile away.

framing.detail: The Pulaski Citizen headed it 'A Raper Lynched' and called the hanging 'quick and sure and dreadful and just', the work of 'good men' with a 'righteous duty'.
The Milan Exchange called it 'a deliberate and cool punishment' and the Winchester Home Journal closed 'So mote it be.'

Papers from Washington to Sacramento ran the short Prospect wire under heads such as 'Lynched', 'Short Shrift', 'A Colored Brute Lynched' and 'A Sable Fiend Lynched', and the Evening Critic added a mocking Guiteau headline.
Syndicated roundups reduced it to one line: lynched at Elkton 'for an outrage upon a white woman'.
